paras: The threatened lynching of Tom Carrington took place at Chatham, Virginia, in early September 1881, when a crowd at his examination on a charge of assaulting his fifteen-year-old stepdaughter repeatedly threatened to lynch him. Carrington asked the officers to protect him, and no violence against him was reported. The episode is known from a single Richmond telegram, which attributed the threats to "the negroes present."

According to the telegram, "a few days" before it was printed, a woman described as "a negro woman" ran into the town of Chatham and told Sheriff Overby that her husband, Tom Carrington, had nearly beaten to death and "brutally outraged" her daughter by her first husband. The dispatch placed the town in "Pittsburgh county."

The sheriff sent deputy sheriffs Jesse J. Overby and J. Doran Hunt to the farm of James M. Whittle, where they found Carrington in a tobacco barn and brought him back to town. Justice William L. Lewis began the examination at once, and the evidence presented accused Carrington of throwing the girl down, beating her "until she was black and blue," and raping her.

A large crowd attended the hearing, and the telegram said that threats of lynching "were frequently expressed by the negroes present." Described as "frightened almost to death," Carrington asked the officers to protect him from "the vengeance of the crowd."
Justice Lewis sent Carrington to the county court to answer an indictment. No report of a trial or of any further threat against him appears in the coverage.

The Washington Evening Star printed the Richmond telegram on 14 September 1881 under the headline "A Fiend in Jail." The dispatch called the case "a horrible story," referred to the prisoner as "the fiend," and reported the lynching threats as an expression of popular "indignation" without comment on them. No other newspaper account of the case appears in the coverage.
